# ENVIRONMENT and DISASTER MANAGEMENT

🟢 Learn (asked in PYQs or in the water / coast / DM clusters) · 🟡 Answer-ready (not asked yet, but must be able to write on it: definition + 2 named examples + India's response + challenges + way forward) · ⚪ Skip (background, history)

<toggle heading="h1">
1\. CONSERVATION

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Overview

- 20% foresrts are under protection of state departments more than the Aichi target 11 (The Aichi Biodiversity Targets are a set of 20 global goals established in 2010 to combat the loss of biodiversity. They were part of the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020, adopted by the parties of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) during the COP10 summit in Nagoya, Aichi Prefecture, Japan.) (target 11 : This is often considered the most famous Aichi Target. It aimed to protect: 17% of terrestrial and inland water areas 10% of coastal and marine area)
- Carrying capacity : the most individuals (or resource use) an area can support for ever without degrading its resources (Exceeded → resources run down (aquifers, rivers, grass) + sudden population crash + overshoot lowers the area's future capacity (overfished lake never gets its fish back even after fishing stops) + Used in planning: carrying-capacity studies for hill towns (SC asked Himalayan states for one, 2023) + caps on tourists and vehicles + basis for EIA and master plans (eg. Joshimath sinking 2023 = capacity ignored)
- <b>Examples</b>: Kaziranga, Assam (worked: one-horned rhino \~200 in 1905 → 2,600+ in 2022 via strict <span color="green_bg">protected area</span> + anti-poaching) + Great Indian Bustard, Rajasthan (failed: under 150 left, power-line collisions → SC 2021 ordered lines underground)
- <b>India's response</b>: PAs on 5.71% of land + Project Tiger / Elephant + <span color="green_bg">NBSAP 2024–30</span> + Biological Diversity Act + carrying-capacity studies for hill towns
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Criteria for Biodiversity hotspots

<toggle>
<b>Why biodiversity varies across India</b>

Varies because: latitude 8°–37°N (tropical Kerala → temperate J&K) + rainfall 100 mm → 11,000 mm (Cherrapunji); wet Western Ghats vs dry Deccan rain shadow only \~100 km apart + 11,000 km coast and big rivers + islands cut off → endemism (Andamans, Lakshadweep) + old Gondwana block → long time to evolve + Northeast = meeting point of 3 realms (Indian, Indo-Malayan, Indo-Chinese)
</toggle>

- 1\. Species Richness: The region must have at least <span color="green_bg">1,500 species of vascular plants</span> as endemics.
- 2\. Threat Level: The region must have lost at least <span color="green_bg">70% of its original habitat</span>, indicating a high level of threat and a critical need for conservation attention
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Western Ghats

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: The Western Ghats, a key <span color="green_bg">biodiversity hotspot</span>
- <b>Significance</b>: UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) + source of Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri + brings monsoon rain to the peninsula (<span color="green_bg">water tower</span> of south India)
- <b>Examples</b>: Wayanad landslide, Jul 2024 (failed: villages in the Gadgil-flagged zone, quarrying + building on steep slopes) + Silent Valley, Kerala (1984, worked: people's campaign stopped a dam → National Park)
- <b>India's response</b>: Conservation efforts include ESA designations by the <span color="green_bg">Gadgil</span> (2011) and (increaising Economically sensitive area (ESA) designtion to 37% land) <span color="green_bg">Kasturirangan</span> (2013) Committees, community-led forest protection through JFM (joint forest management, and the Western Ghats Biosphere Reserve to balance ecological protection with sustainable development.
- <b>Challenges</b>: face threats from deforestation, mining, and infrastructure projects + Western Ghats <span color="green_bg">ESA</span> draft notification reissued 6 times since 2014, still not final (states object)
- <b>Way forward</b>: finalise the ESA notification with states on board + no quarrying or building on steep slopes + community-led protection (JFM, BMCs)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 COP 16 UN Convention on Biological Diversity

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Location: Cali, Colombia \| Theme: "Peace with Nature"
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Key Outcomes & Frameworks
  - The <span color="green_bg">Cali Fund</span> (DSI Mechanism): A landmark "benefit-sharing" agreement.
    - Requirement: Large companies (pharmaceutical, cosmetic, biotech) using <span color="green_bg">Digital Sequence Information</span> (DSI) from genetic resources must contribute to the fund.
  - Contribution: 1% of profits or 0.1% of revenue.
  - Beneficiaries: Funds are directed toward Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs) for biodiversity conservation.
  - Institutional Recognition: A new permanent subsidiary body was established to ensure the effective participation of Indigenous peoples in CBD processes.
  - Kunming Biodiversity Fund: Formally launched to support developing nations in hitting biodiversity targets.
  - Marine Conservation: Identification of "Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Areas" (EBSAs) to help achieve the <span color="green_bg">30-by-30</span> goal.
  - Technical Progress: Action plans were advanced regarding synthetic biology, management of invasive species, and the "One Health" approach (linking biodiversity to human health).
- <b>Examples</b>: Cali Fund (launched Feb 2025; first private payment only in Nov 2025, a small UK startup → voluntary model weak) + Protected Planet Report released at Cali (17.6% land, 8.4% ocean protected → far from <span color="green_bg">30x30</span>)
- <b>India's response</b>: released updated <span color="green_bg">NBSAP</span> at Cali (Oct 2024) → 23 national targets matched to KMGBF + <span color="green_bg">Whole of Government, Whole of Society</span> + asked for international finance to implement it → one of only 44 countries to submit by the end of COP16 (see 🟡 India – NBSAP 2024–30)
- <b>Challenges</b>: Cali Fund payments are voluntary + COP16 ran out of quorum on finance and had to resume in Rome (Feb 2025)
- <b>Way forward</b>: make DSI payments binding + close the <span color="green_bg">finance gap</span> + implement NBSAPs on time
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF)

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Aims to halt biodiversity loss or reverse by 2030 (adopted at CBD COP15, Montreal, Dec 2022)
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: 23 targets by 2030 like 30% land and sea conservation and halving invasive species + promote fair benefit-sharing (including via DSI)
- <b>Significance</b>: new global targets after the 2010 <span color="green_bg">Aichi targets</span> were missed (none of the 20 fully met by 2020)
- <b>Examples</b>: Protected Planet Report 2024 (failed so far: protection must double on land and triple at sea by 2030) + Salas y Gómez–Nazca ridges, SE Pacific (Chile-led, set to be among the first high-seas MPAs → helps Target 3)
- <b>India's response</b>: updated NBSAP (Oct 2024) maps India's 23 targets onto KMGBF's 23 + <span color="green_bg">30x30</span> via PAs, community reserves and OECMs + biodiversity finance via BIOFIN (see 🟡 India – NBSAP 2024–30)
- <b>Challenges</b>: close the \$700 billion finance gap
- <b>Way forward</b>: fund the targets (Cali Fund, Kunming Fund) + honest progress reports in each national report
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 India – NBSAP 2024–30

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Alignment: Fully aligned with the <span color="green_bg">Kunming-Montreal</span> Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). + Core Objective: Halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030; "Living in Harmony with Nature" by 2050.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>
  - Targets: 23 National Biodiversity Targets (NBTs) across three pillars: Threat Reduction, Sustainable Use, and Implementation Tools.
  - Approach: "Whole-of-Government" (23 ministries involved) and "Whole-of-Society" (incorporating Indigenous/local knowledge).
  - Finance: Supported by the Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN); estimated annual requirement of ₹81,664 crore.
  - Mechanism: Three-tier governance (NBA → SBB → BMC) under the BD Act 2002 (amended 2023).
- <b>Significance (India's status)</b>
  - India recently submitted 7th national report under article 26 of convention on biological diversity
  - all 23 revised NBSAP indicators are on track and align with KMGBF
  - Forest + tree cover = 25.1 % of geographical area
  - Forest carbon stock reached 7,285.5 million tonnes (55% is soil organic carbon)
  - 24.1 million hectares (mha) restored or under restoration (<span color="green_bg">Bonn Challenge</span> pledge of 26 mha by 2030)
  - 100 <span color="green_bg">Ramsar</span> sites as of Jun 2026 (26 in 2014). (Ranks 1st in Asia and 3rd globally).
  - Wildlife Populations: 3,682 Tigers (>70% of global total), 22,446 Elephants, >4,000 Rhinos, and 891 Asiatic Lions.
    - First Assessments: Recorded 718 Snow Leopards and 6,327 Riverine Dolphins.
  - Protected Areas covers 5.71% of land area; marine protected areas have also increase
- <b>Examples</b>: Arittapatti, Madurai (worked: Tamil Nadu's first <span color="green_bg">Biodiversity Heritage Site</span>, 2022 → Centre cancelled a tungsten mining block there after protests, Jan 2025) + Project Cheetah, Kuno NP (2022, mixed: species recovery target, but many cheetah deaths in the first year)
- <b>India's response</b>: India implements by using PARVESH for green clearance, for eco sys restore (Bonn challenge (restore 26 million degraded land) , species recovery & genetic diversity (via species recovery program) + sustainable agriculture via natural and organic farming + Pollution reduction via national clean air programme + Urban ecosystem ( smart cities) + Access and benefit sharing via (Nagoya protocol mechanism) + Finance (CSR and Business responsibility and sustainability report (top 1000 firms) ) + capacity building via national one health mission
- <b>Challenges</b>: finance (₹81,664 crore a year needed) + many BMCs exist only on paper + species recovery mixed (cheetah deaths)
- <b>Way forward</b>: BIOFIN + CSR money for targets + empower <span color="green_bg">BMCs</span> and People's Biodiversity Registers + track all 23 targets in the 8th national report
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Case study of eco-bridge a.k.a eco ducts

- Madhya Pradesh-Maharashtra Border Eco-Underpass: This eco-bridge will be one of India's longest underpasses, stretching across 1.4 kilometers. Situated on the Madhya Pradesh-Maharashtra border, the project is designed to support wildlife movement and enhance conservation efforts in the area
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 People’s movements

- The <span color="green_bg">Chipko</span> Movement (1973) in Uttarakhand used non-violent resistance to stop deforestation, leading to a ban on commercial logging in the Himalayas.
- Inspired by it, the Appiko Movement (1983) in Karnataka promoted tree conservation through direct action.
- The Anti-Tehri Dam Movement (1980s–1990s) opposed the Tehri Dam over its severe environmental and social impacts.
- <span color="green_bg">Narmada Bachao</span> Andolan (1985–Present)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 WPA issues and features

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 = India's main law for wild animals, plants and their habitats (amended 2022) + Art 48A (DPSP) + Art 51A(g) + Concurrent List
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: The New Scheduling System (Post-2022 Amendment): The 2022 Amendment streamlined the schedules from six down to four, simplifying enforcement and legal proceedings:

| Schedule | Scope & Protection Level | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule I | Highest Protection: Absolute protection with the highest penalties. | Tigers, Elephants, Lions |
| Schedule II | High Protection: Significant species but with slightly lower penalties than Sch. I. | Various birds and reptiles |
| Schedule III | Protected Plants: Specific flora species requiring conservation. | Red Sanders, Beddomes' Cycad |
| Schedule IV | <span color="green_bg">CITES</span> Species: Species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species. | Exotic birds/animals in trade |

- Protected Areas (PA) Hierarchy
  - The Act provides a tiered approach to habitat protection, currently covering approximately 5.26% of India's landmass (now 5.71%, Mains 365):
  - National Parks (NPs): No human activity or grazing is permitted. Highest level of restriction.
  - Wildlife Sanctuaries (WLS): Certain rights (grazing, collection of minor forest produce) can be allowed by the Chief Wildlife Warden.
  - Conservation Reserves: Publicly owned land acting as "buffer zones" or corridors between existing NPs/WLS.
  - Community Reserves: Private or community land where locals volunteer to protect biodiversity.
- Statutory Enforcement Bodies
  - <span color="green_bg">NBWL</span> (National Board for Wildlife): Chaired by the Prime Minister; the apex body for policy and project clearances in PAs.
  - NTCA (National Tiger Conservation Authority): Oversees "Project Tiger" and management of Tiger Reserves.
  - WCCB (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau): Intelligence and enforcement agency for organized wildlife crime.
  - CZA (Central Zoo Authority): Regulatory body for all zoos and captive breeding standards.
- <b>Significance</b>: Success Figures: The Act has successfully increased flagship species—Tigers (3,682, up from 2,967) and Elephants are both on the rise. + PAs 5.71% with 106 National Parks (Dec 2024) + tigers >70% of world (Mar 2026) + 22,446 elephants + TX2 met in 2018, 4 years early
- <b>Examples</b>: Kaziranga (worked: zero rhino poaching in 2022, first time since 1977) + <span color="green_bg">Great Indian Bustard</span> (failed: Schedule I since 1972, yet only \~130 left, WII 2025)
- <b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">Project Tiger</span> (1973) + Project Elephant (1992) + Project Cheetah (2022) + WCCB for wildlife crime + <span color="green_bg">IBCA</span> (HQ India) + IDWH scheme + DNA lab at WII + Project Tiger 50 years (2023)
- <b>Challenges</b>: Current Challenges & Critical Analysis
  - A. Enforcement & Legal Gaps
    - Illegal Trade: Despite WCCB efforts, local trade remains a loophole. Evidence: The recent seizure of 100+ birds and turtles in Jalaun proves that grassroots enforcement is still weak.
    - Unscientific Interventions: There is a rise in "enforcement abuses" where private actors (like snake catchers) use unscientific methods or engage in price gouging. Kerala’s recent blacklisting of such catchers highlights the need for a standardized protocol.
  - B. Human-Wildlife Conflict (HWC) & Federalism
    - The "Vermin" Debate: Rising conflicts (boars, macaques) have led to State-Centre tensions. States like Keralademand the power to declare vermin for culling, but the Centre resists delegating this power to prevent ecological misuse.
    - Urban Wildlife: Poor management in cities like Gurgaon (e.g., illegal use of langurs to drive away monkeys) shows a lack of policy for wildlife outside traditional forests.
    - HWC: 1,630 people killed by animals (ADSI 2024) + Kerala declared HWC a <span color="green_bg">state-specific disaster</span> + human–elephant conflict rising (Jharkhand, West Bengal) + zoonoses (Nipah) + crop loss + retaliatory killing
  - C. Success vs. Carrying Capacity
    - The Dilemma: Higher populations in a restricted 5% PA network inevitably lead to higher human-wildlife friction as animals move into human-dominated landscapes.
  - D. Other: \~10 mn ha forest lost a year (WWF) + rhinos, pangolins worst hit by wildlife crime (2024) + wildlife down 73% since 1970 (Living Planet Report)
- <b>Way forward</b>: wildlife <span color="green_bg">corridors</span> beyond the 5% PA network + a standard protocol for rescuers + clear Centre–State rules on vermin + stronger local enforcement + HWC: National HWC Mitigation Strategy & Action Plan 2021–26 + SOPs (tiger, leopard, elephant) + early warnings (SMS, sensors, GPS collars) + <span color="green_bg">bee-hive fences</span>, solar fences + crops elephants avoid (chilli, citrus, ginger) + SC: ₹10 lakh for human deaths + landscape approach + NGOs (WPSI, WTI)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ NWAP

- Landscape Approach, Mainstreaming Climate Resilience, People-centric Conservation, Integration with Development Planning(EIA), Focus on Marine Biodiversity
- Issues w NWAP : Non-binding in nature—lack of legal enforceability, Poor inter-departmental coordination, Human-wildlife conflict mitigation efforts remain fragmented and reactive, Inadequate funding and manpower for monitoring actions
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: amends 42 central laws (incl. EPA 1986 and Air Act 1981) to replace jail with penalties for minor offences
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>
  - 1\. <span color="green_bg">Decriminalized minor offences</span>: Actions like polluting beyond limits or not furnishing required information are no longer criminal; they're now civil violations—with penalties.
  - 2\. Set up Adjudicating Officers: Specialized officers handle violations and determine penalties instead of courts.
  - 3\. Introduction of <span color="green_bg">Environmental Protection Fund</span>: Fines collected go directly into a dedicated fund used for environmental projects.
- <b>Significance</b>: <span color="green_bg">ease of doing business</span> + fewer cases in courts
- <b>Examples</b>: EPA Section 15 (2023: jail → penalty of ₹10,000 to ₹15 lakh, fixed by an <span color="green_bg">adjudicating officer</span>) + Water (Amendment) Act 2024 (same shift for the Water Act)
- <b>India's response</b>: 4. Jan Vishwas 2.0 is being planned to introduce to decorum other provisions around 250 with penalties to reduce compliance related delay and log cost
- <b>Challenges</b>: Issues
  - Supreme Court deems the Act “<span color="green_bg">toothless</span>” post amendments—criminal provisions dropped, enforcement stalled
  - Ongoing environmental harms: polluted Futala Lake (Nagpur), palm tree felling in Bihar leading to lightning deaths; Even if an EIA report is negative-still go ahead is given, Persistent issues: illegal quarrying in Kerala forests, oil spill near Kochi, heavy metal air pollution in Delhi, state EIA not appointed on time.
- <b>Way forward</b>: fines high enough to deter + quick adjudication + keep criminal liability for serious harm
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 The Biological Diversity Act, 2002

- Protects India’s plants, animals, and traditional knowledge by regulating access, preventing biopiracy, and ensuring fair benefit-sharing through a <span color="green_bg">three-tier</span> institutional framework: NBA 9National Biodiversity Authority), SBBs (State Biodiversity Boards)(28 in number), and BMCs (Biodiversity Management Committees) (1.4 lakh).
- Promotes conservation (can be declared <span color="green_bg">Biodiversity Heritage Sites</span> (BHS) for protection eg Kaya Kalp Vriksh (Punjab) — a giant, old tree of cultural and ecological importance. Mangroves in Gujarat — preserved for their role in coastal protection and biodiversity.), sustainable use, and equitable sharing of benefits from biodiversity resources and promotes NGT working (eg. Nayar River case (June 2025)).
- Recent amendments (2023) weakened enforcement by decriminalizing offences and exempting AYUSH practitioners, reducing local community benefits (The 2025 regulations set benefit-sharing rates from 0.2–0.6% for most resources and 5%+ for high-value ones, included <span color="green_bg">Digital Sequence Information</span> (DSI), reduced community shares to 85–90%, and let NBA/SBBs retain funds if providers are unknown)
- The 2025 regulations expanded scope to digital genetic data but enforcement remains weak (especially Nagoya protocol (The Nagoya Protocol is an international agreement that ensures fair sharing of benefits when genetic resources (like plants or animals) are used. India struggles with its implementation due to weak enforcement, lack of awareness, and bureaucratic delays but the recent The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 modernizes India’s biodiversity laws by expanding resource definitions, easing research and traditional medicine use (Indian entities must register with NBA if research based patent), and shifting from jail terms to fines.
- It also clarifies NBA and SBB roles, strengthens patent rules, and broadens exemptions for domestic users via exemptions for AYUSH therefore bringing it closer to Nagoya.
- NBA's new ABS framework: resource from an identifiable institution → 25–40% of ABS money to it, 60–75% to local communities via SBBs/UTBCs + from traders (origin unknown) → spent straight on conservation + digital records for traceability
- BMCs keep People's Biodiversity Registers (local biodiversity + traditional knowledge)
- Overall, India has strong laws and institutions but faces challenges in fair implementation and protecting tribal rights.
- <b>Examples</b>: Kani tribe, Kerala (1990s, worked: Jeevani drug from arogyapacha → licence fee and royalty shared with the tribe = early <span color="green_bg">access and benefit sharing</span> model) + Bt brinjal, Karnataka (2011, failed: NBA case against Mahyco/Monsanto for using local brinjal varieties without approval → dragged on for years = <span color="green_bg">biopiracy</span> hard to punish)
- Genetic resources & TK: TK examples: karez/surang bavi water harvesting (Bidar) + sacred groves (Khasi, Garo) + Soligas managing BRT Tiger Reserve → protected by <span color="green_bg">TKDL</span> + Patents Act 1970 + PPVFR Act 2001 + GI Act 1999 + AYUSH ministry + Yoga on UNESCO list → problems: biopiracy, poor records, weak farmer rights → way forward: pay TK holders + teach TK + ABS under Nagoya
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Forests

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Forest (21% of geographical area) + 3rd in avg annual net gain (state of worlds forests report) + forest + tree cover <span color="green_bg">25.17%</span> (ISFR 2023; 24.62% in 2021) + \~2% of world forest area (GFRA 2025)
  - Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)’s Global Forest Resources Assessment (GFRA) 2025 released on 22 October 2025
    - 9th position worldwide in terms of total forest area
    - 3 rd in net gain
    - Bamboo Plantations: The total bamboo resource globally is estimated at 30.1 million ha, of which 21.2 million ha (70 percent) is in Asia, with India accounting for 11.8 million hectares
    - Rubber Plantations: India ranks 5th globally with 831 thousand hectares of rubber plantations
    - Agroforestry Area: India, along with Indonesia, accounts for nearly 100% of Asia’s agroforestry area
    - As per 2025 Forest Resources Assessment, the world’s forests acted as a net <span color="green_bg">carbon sink</span> during the 2021–2025 period, sequestering 3.6 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide (Gt CO2) annually on forest land.
- <b>Significance</b>: 12000 tonnes of CO2 sink + livelihood to 275 million + carbon stock \~24,000 mt CO₂ worth \~\$120 bn + shield against storms and floods (mangroves, coastal forests) + NTFPs (SOFO 2024)
- <b>Examples</b>: Sukhomajri, Haryana (1970s–80s, worked: village protected the Shivalik catchment in return for water and grass rights → model for <span color="green_bg">Joint Forest Management</span>) + Hasdeo Arand, Chhattisgarh (2022 on, failed: coal mining in dense forest despite gram sabha protests)
- <b>India's response</b>: (green forest mission : increase by 5Mha ) + ( Miyazaki method of forest regeneration (regenerate based on specified locality) + Initiatives that led to this : National Mission for a Green India (GIM) (Aims to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million ha ), <span color="green_bg">Mission LiFE</span> (Lifestyle for Environment) (ek pedh ma ke naam) + NDC: extra <span color="green_bg">carbon sink</span> of 3.5–4.0 bn t CO₂e by 2035 (from 2005) + Bonn Challenge 26 Mha by 2030 + National Afforestation Programme + CAMPA
- <b>Challenges</b>: deforestation 3.3 % b/w 2001-2022 + forest land diverted for mining (Hasdeo) + forest finance gap \$216 bn to 2030 (UNEP 2025) + \~77% of world's mines within 50 km of Key Biodiversity Areas + warming → more forest fires
- <b>Way forward</b>: native-species planting with survival audits + community forest rights + <span color="green_bg">REDD+</span> finance for standing forests (UNFCCC COP13) + restoration (rehabilitation, reclamation) + best practices (Japan's Forest Environment Tax, Congo Basin Forest Partnership) + rights-based approach
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Indian Forest Act, 1927

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: The Core Philosophy: This is a <span color="green_bg">colonial-era law</span>. Its primary goal was to extract timber and generate revenue by giving the State absolute monopoly over forests, viewing local tribes as obstacles.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Classifies forests into <span color="green_bg">Reserved, Protected, Village</span>, and Private categories, giving the government strict control over forest resources and activities like logging and grazing. + It criminalizes unauthorized use with penalties and empowers forest officers to enforce laws and seize illegal property.
- <b>Significance</b>: provides strong legal authority to prevent encroachment
- <b>Examples</b>: Draft IFA amendment, 2019 (failed: arms and immunity for forest officers → withdrawn Nov 2019 after tribal protests) + bamboo amendment, 2017 (worked: bamboo grown outside forests cut and sold without transit permits)
- <b>India's response</b>: removal of bamboo classification as a tree in 2017 eases local use
- <b>Challenges</b>: enforcement lapses (Over 10,000 acres recently encroached in Odisha’s Reserved Forests amid enforcement lapses.) have led to large-scale illegal activities and conflicts with tribal rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 + The Act’s restrictions historically limited tribal economic benefits
- <b>Way forward</b>: align with <span color="green_bg">FRA</span> (Gram Sabha say) + digitise forest records + conservation over revenue
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: The Core Philosophy: Post-independence, India realized its forests were vanishing rapidly. This act shifted power from the States to the Center to stop the indiscriminate diversion of forest land for industries.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Requires central government approval for diverting forest land to non-forestry uses and mandates <span color="green_bg">compensatory afforestation</span>, wildlife clearance, and catchment protection.
  - It broadly defines “forest land,” includes recognition of tribal rights under the Forest Rights Act (FRA), and is enforced by MoEFCC with <span color="green_bg">Gram Sabha</span> and state oversight.
- <b>Significance</b>: Positives include regulated forest land use and institutionalized compensatory afforestation (non-forest penalty was introduced) + CA: 85% of target met (2019–24, CEC) under CAF Act 2016 (<span color="green_bg">CAMPA</span>, from Godavarman)
- <b>Examples</b>: <span color="green_bg">T.N. Godavarman</span> (1996, worked: SC read 'forest' by its dictionary meaning → FCA applied to all forests, not just recorded ones) + Gachibowli, Hyderabad (2025, failed): The Gachibowli case highlighted conflicts between urban development and ecological protection(The area lies near the KBR National Park <span color="green_bg">Eco-Sensitive Zone</span> (ESZ) and the Biodiversity Park, both critical urban green lungs.), leading to Supreme Court emphasizing ecological sanctity over convenience. (Re: Kancha Gachibowli Forest, State of Telangana)
- <b>India's response</b>: The 2023 Amendment narrows forest land scope (Forest land now includes only areas recorded as forest on or after Oct 25, 1980, unless diverted by Dec 12, 1996.), introduces exemptions for strategic projects, allows eco-tourism and silviculture and safaris and surveys, and strengthens central authority.
- <b>Challenges</b>: issues involve poor survival rates of compensatory plants, uneven FRA implementation, and uncollected penalties for violations. + CA funds: late plans, many state approvals, short staff, misuse
- <b>Way forward</b>: Future actions include ensuring genuine Gram Sabha consultations, improving compensatory afforestation quality, enforcing penalties, auditing forest diversion, and focusing on net ecological benefits. + geo-tag CA sites online (e-Green Watch, PARIVESH 2.0) + regular State CAMPA meetings
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Forest Rights Act, 2006

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Recognizes and restores individual and community rights of Scheduled Tribes and traditional forest dwellers over forest land and resources. It empowers Gram Sabhas to manage and conserve forests sustainably. The Act also overrides conflicting provisions of earlier laws like the Indian Forest Act, 1927.
- <b>Significance</b>: undoes the <span color="green_bg">historical injustice</span> to forest dwellers (Act's preamble) + makes them partners in conservation
- <b>Examples</b>: Case study : Mendha Lekha village in Maharashtra was the first to claim community forest rights under FRA, managing 1,800 hectares sustainably through Gram Sabha, boosting livelihoods and achieving zero deforestation. + <span color="green_bg">Niyamgiri</span>, Odisha (2013, worked: SC let <span color="green_bg">gram sabhas</span> decide → all 12 rejected Vedanta's bauxite mine) + SC eviction order, Feb 2019 (failed: \~11.8 lakh households with rejected claims ordered out → stayed within days; shows high wrongful rejection of claims)
- <b>India's response</b>: FRA cells in tribal districts under Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (2024) to clear pending claims
- <b>Challenges</b>: Issues w it : CFR (<span color="green_bg">Community Forest Resource</span> rights. When a community files a CFR claim, they are making a formal, legal request to the government to recognize and restore their traditional rights to acces) claims pending in 65% of eligible villages (MoTA 2025 report), States like Madhya Pradesh and Odisha continue to bypass <span color="green_bg">Gram Sabha</span> during forest diversion clearance, Commercial plantation projects (e.g. oil palm in NE India, Palm Oil Plantation Row (Assam, 2024–25): Gram Sabha consent bypassed) are being approved without community consent (Assam Palm Oil Row (2024–25)), Legal evictions rise after denial of claims—over 20,000 families affected in Telangana and Chhattisgarh (2024–25), Lack of legal literacy.
- <b>Way forward</b>: time-bound disposal of claims + legal literacy camps + <span color="green_bg">Gram Sabha consent</span> before any diversion
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023:

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: amends the FCA 1980 + renames it Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: 1. Narrowing the Definition of a "Forest" (The Biggest Controversy)
- The Background: In the landmark 1996 T.N. <span color="green_bg">Godavarman</span> Supreme Court case, the court ruled that the word "forest" must be understood according to its dictionary meaning, regardless of who owned the land or whether it was officially recorded as a forest by the government. This protected millions of hectares of unrecorded, natural forests (like the Aravallis, sacred groves, and mangroves).
- The 2023 Change: The amendment explicitly reversed the Supreme Court's ruling. It stated that the strict protections of the Act now only apply to lands that were officially recorded as "forest" in government records on or after October 25, 1980.
- The 100-km Border Exemption (The Security vs. Ecology Debate)
  - The Change: The amendment completely exempts forest land located within 100 kilometers of international borders, the Line of Control (LoC), or the Line of Actual Control (LAC) if the land is needed for "strategic linear projects of national importance" (like highways, railways, or military infrastructure).
- <b>Significance</b>: The Rationale: The government argued this is necessary for rapid troop movement and national security, especially given geopolitical tensions with China.
- <b>Examples</b>: SC interim order, Feb 2024 (worked: states must keep the 1996 <span color="green_bg">dictionary meaning</span> of forest until deemed-forest records are ready) + Aravallis (failed: unrecorded Aravalli scrub forests in Haryana lose protection → see 🟢 ARAVALLIS)
- <b>Challenges</b>
  - The Impact: This effectively strips federal protection from nearly 28% of India's actual forest cover that happens to be unclassified or unrecorded. These lands can now be easily cleared by state governments or sold to private developers for real estate, mining, or industry without needing clearance from the Central Ministry (MoEFCC).
  - The Impact (The Criticism): If you draw a 100-km line inward from all of India's borders, you effectively swallow up almost the entire ecologically fragile North-East India, the high Himalayas, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Environmentalists argue this gives a blank check to bulldoze some of the world's most sensitive biodiversity hotspots without any environmental impact assessments.
- <b>Way forward</b>: finish <span color="green_bg">deemed-forest</span> records state by state + keep the dictionary meaning till then + EIA even for border projects
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Amendment Rules, 2025

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Notified by MoEFCC in late 2025, amends the 2023 framework → heavily prioritizes "ease of doing business," strategic infrastructure and resource security, though it has sparked considerable debate among ecologists. Here is the structured breakdown:
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: 1. "Working Permission" for Linear Projects: earlier both Stage-I (in-principle) and Stage-II (final) clearances were needed before any work → The Change: states can grant "working permission" right after Stage-I for railway tracks, transmission lines, initial roadwork (not black-topping or concretization) → Impact: drastically speeds up mobilization of labor and site preparation
- 2\. The Critical Minerals Carve-Out: global race for lithium, cobalt → critical and strategic mineral mines (MMDR Act list) can raise <span color="green_bg">Compensatory Afforestation</span> (CA) over degraded forest land (at least double the diverted area) + EIA Exemption: no mandatory Public Consultation
- 3\. Dilution of CA Rigidity: CA land earlier had to be notified as "Protected Forest" (Indian Forest Act, 1927) → now optional, only mutated in revenue records to the Forest Department + "land banking" + states can use central afforestation schemes to meet CA targets
- 4\. Extended Timelines & Offline Approvals: Stage-I validity 2 → 5 years + offline applications (bypassing PARIVESH) for defense, emergencies and vaguely defined "projects of national importance"
- 6\. Allowing Commercial Activities (Eco-Tourism & Safaris): the 2023 amendment made zoos, safaris and eco-tourism "forestry activities" → states can clear trees for hotels, paved roads and safari infrastructure without central oversight → revenue, but concrete, noise pollution and human-wildlife conflict in pristine habitats (Eg. Aravalli issue)
- <b>Examples</b>: critical, strategic and atomic mineral mines exempted from <span color="green_bg">public hearings</span> (Sep 2025) + "public utility" left undefined → diversions easier (Mongabay, Apr 2026)
- <b>Challenges</b>: 5. The Ecological Criticism: streamlines bottlenecks but severe red flags → Legal Shield Weakened (CA land without Protected Forest notification lacks the hard legal armor against future diversion) + Supreme Court Friction (bypasses the spirit of SC's early 2025 interim orders: no net reduction in actual, ground-level forest land)
- <b>Way forward</b>: notify CA land as Protected Forest + public consultation even for critical-mineral mines + all approvals on PARIVESH + <span color="green_bg">no net loss</span> of forest, as the SC asked
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 ARAVALLIS

- Oldest fold mountains (Pre-Cambrian, older than the Himalayas), \~692 km running south-west: Delhi → Haryana → Rajasthan → Gujarat
- Why it matters: wall stopping the Thar from moving east + minerals (Khetri copper) + culture (Dilwara temples) + people lived here since the Palaeolithic (Mangar Bani)
- Definition row: SC in the <span color="green_bg">Godavarman</span> case asked for one definition (May 2024) → Nov 2025 SC accepted it: hill = 100 m above the surrounding land, range = 2+ hills within 500 m. Mining plan on the Saranda model (<span color="green_bg">Go / No-Go</span> zones) → Dec 2025 Centre bans new mining leases (except critical, strategic and atomic minerals) → Dec 2025 SC stays its own order after protests and orders a fresh review
- Why protests: low hills lose protection → mining and construction → desert spreads + groundwater crisis
- Challenges: minerals vs ecology + illegal construction (Aravalli safari, Haryana) + every state uses its own definition (in silos)
- Protection: <span color="green_bg">Aravalli Green Wall</span> (5 km buffer, 4 states) + Mangar Bani no-construction zone (Haryana 2016) + MC Mehta case (2002) + Save Aravalli Movement (Rajendra Singh → SC halted Sariska mining, 1990)
- Way forward: treat it as one continuous ridge + transparent data + strict mining bans in sensitive zones

<quote>
<p />

MINING hazards: forest and land lost + acid mine drainage and heavy metals in water + groundwater falls + dust → lung disease + land subsidence and underground fires (Jharia) + tailings dams can burst + tribal displacement<br />Eg: Jharia coal fires + Goa and Bellary iron ore (illegal mining, SC bans) + Aravallis (above info)

<toggle color="purple_bg">
Go / No-Go zones

Go / No-Go (MoEF + Coal Ministry, 2009–10): coal blocks in 9 coalfields split into "Go" (mining allowed) and "No-Go" (dense forest: >30% gross or >10% weighted forest cover) → roughly a third of blocks were No-Go → diluted later ("inviolate forest" idea) under pressure for coal

<br />Modern version: SC in Saranda (2025) made Jharkhand declare a wildlife sanctuary and ordered a mining plan with Go / No-Go zones from geo-referenced ecological mapping → same model asked for the Aravallis
</toggle>

<br />Remedies: EIA + Go/No-Go zones + progressive and final mine closure plans + reclaim and afforest mined land + DMF / PMKKKY (info also in RE toggle) for affected people + star rating of mines + drones and satellite checks on illegal mining
</quote>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Sacred groves

- MoEFCC (2025) initiated discussions to include “Sacred Groves” under community reserves for enhanced legal protection via amendments to the Wildlife Protection Act, Kerala Biodiversity Board in April 2025 launched a digitization drive to map 1,200+ groves using GIS and drone surveys, Tribal Ministry's push to integrate sacred groves into India's carbon sequestration goals, aligning with Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), UNESCO recognition (March 2025): India’s sacred groves network nominated as “Traditional Conservation Landscape” under the cultural-ecological heritage category.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 International conventions

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: global treaties that protect species, habitats and genetic resources across borders
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: <span color="green_bg">CITES</span> (1973) protects endangered species by regulating international trade to prevent threats like poaching.
- CMS (1979) conserves migratory species across borders through legal frameworks.
- The UN Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) promotes biodiversity conservation and sustainable use, including Access and Benefit Sharing. It also has COP, recent COP 15 adopted The <span color="green_bg">Kunming-Montreal</span> Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), adopted in December 2022 at CBD COP 15, sets global goals to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, including conserving 30% of land and oceans, restoring 30% of degraded ecosystems, reducing invasive species and pollution by half, and cutting \$500 billion in harmful subsidies. It emphasizes inclusive governance (rights of indigenous), equitable benefit-sharing, and mobilizing \$200 billion annually for biodiversity. Called the "<span color="green_bg">Paris Agreement</span> for Nature," it aims for a nature-positive future, with progress reviews at COP16 in 2024.
- The Man and Biosphere Programme (1971) fosters sustainable development via establishment of biosphere reserves
- PGRFA (plant genetic resources for food and agriculture) focuses on preserving plant genetic resources vital for food security and crop improvement. + ITPGRFA (2001, India a member): shares 64 crops and forages = \~80% of plant diet + Lima meeting (GB-11, 2025): benefit-sharing talks failed, DSI rules pushed to next meeting + India: protect sovereign rights + DSI risk = digital biopiracy (Cali Fund set up for it)
- <b>Examples</b>: CITES CoP18, 2019 (worked: India got the star tortoise and smooth-coated otter moved to Appendix I) + CMS COP13, Gandhinagar 2020 (Great Indian Bustard, Asian elephant, Bengal florican added to Appendix I)
- <b>India's response</b>: party to <span color="green_bg">CITES</span> (1976), CMS (1983; hosted CMS COP13, Gandhinagar 2020), CBD (1994) + 18 biosphere reserves, most in UNESCO's MAB network + Wildlife Crime Control Bureau enforces CITES
- <b>Challenges</b>: weak enforcement (illegal wildlife trade) + finance gap + targets not binding (Aichi missed)
- <b>Way forward</b>: matching domestic law (WPA Schedule IV = CITES) + finance for the South + <span color="green_bg">benefit-sharing</span> that reaches local communities
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Ecologically sensitive area

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Declared around protected areas under EPA + notified by the Centre (EPA 1986) → activities: Prohibited (commercial mining, polluting industry) / Regulated (tree felling, hotels) / Permitted (local farming)
- <b>Significance</b>: <span color="green_bg">shock absorber</span> around PAs + protects endemics and water sources
- <b>Examples</b>: Mahabaleshwar–Panchgani <span color="green_bg">Eco-Sensitive Zone</span> (2001, worked: curbs on hill-station construction) + SC order, Jun 2022 (mixed: 1-km ESZ around every PA → relaxed Apr 2023 after states objected) + <span color="green_bg">Netala bypass</span>, Bhagirathi ESZ (2025, failed: Uttarakhand gave in-principle nod though the SC's high-powered committee had rejected it)
- <b>India's response</b>: MoEF&CC issued a draft notification for Western Ghats as an <span color="green_bg">Eco-Sensitive Zone</span> to protect its rich biodiversity, <span color="green_bg">endemic</span> species (50% of India’s amphibians and 67% of fish species are endemic to this region, e.g., Nilgiri Tahr.), and water resources. + <span color="green_bg">RFCTLARR Act 2013</span> (Social Impact Assessment) + FRA 2006 + CAF Act 2016 + DMF 2015
- <b>Challenges</b>: Key challenges include anthropogenic pressures, climate change impacts, and state opposition + Karnataka rejected the <span color="green_bg">Kasturirangan</span> Committee’s proposal to declare 37% (\~60,000 sq km) of the Western Ghats as Eco-sensitive Areas (ESAs), citing development concerns. + >40% of tribals displaced by development + top-down decisions + locals depend on forests for income
- <b>Way forward</b>: suggested measures involve a Western Ghats Ecology Authority, Sustainable Development Fund, and enhanced public participation. + region-wise planning (Himalaya, coast, drylands) + fast-track NGT + social audits + green livelihoods (eco-tourism, bamboo) + Just Transition Fund (SC, <span color="green_bg">Auroville Foundation</span> case: pursue development and environment together)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Great Nicobar Island Project

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: GREAT NICOBAR PROJECT (NITI Aayog idea, Cabinet 2021, nodal agency ANIIDCO)
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Has: transshipment port (Galathea Bay) + airport + 450 MW power plant + township
- <b>Significance</b>: Why: near Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits → cargo + defence
- <b>Examples</b>: NGT, Apr 2023 (mixed: upheld the clearances but set up a high-powered committee → cleared the port again, Feb 2026) + Vizhinjam, Kerala (2025: India's first deep-water <span color="green_bg">transshipment port</span> → the cargo case Great Nicobar builds on)
- <b>Challenges</b>: Concerns: Shompen (PVTG) + Nicobarese displaced, disease risk for Shompen + leatherback turtle nesting at Galathea + \~9.6 lakh trees cut + mangrove belt lost + sits on the megathrust that caused the 2004 tsunami
  - News: forest rights not settled under FRA. A&N admin says the Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Act 1956 is enough → PAT lets the admin divert land alone; FRA needs <span color="green_bg">Gram Sabha</span> consent
- <b>Way forward</b>: phased + ecologically sensitive + community-inclusive
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Wetland conservation

- 6 % of land but cover 40% of global biodev, in india 7 lakh wetland covering 16 MHA (4.86% of area) but India lost 2 of 5 wetlands in 3 decades (Wetlands International)
- The <span color="green_bg">Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017</span> mandate State Wetland Authorities, a National Wetland Committee, digital wetland inventories, and notification of wetlands of national importance. They prohibit harmful activities like reclamation, pollution, and encroachment while promoting <span color="green_bg">wise use</span>, sustainable management, and community awareness.
- For the 2023 PYQ: National Wetland Conservation Programme (1985–86) + National Lake Conservation Plan merged into NPCA (2013) + 2024 "Wetland Wise Use" framework + Centre for Wetland Conservation and Management + Mission Sahbhagita + Save Wetlands Campaign + 12 Blue Flag beaches
- In 2020 130 wetlands identified under national plan for conservation of aquatic ecosystems
- Party to <span color="green_bg">Ramsar</span> Convention (India became a party in 1982 + max sites at Tamil Nadu and followed by Uttar Pradesh)
- Main problems: geographical (invasive species eg. Water hyacith ) + environmental (sustainable extraction is not there ) + (unregulated (governance) + CC (leads to complete submersion or algal bloom)
- RAMSAR CONVENTION (total sites 100; newest: Jai Prakash Narain BS, Shekha Jheel, Patna BS in UP + Chhari-Dhand, Gujarat) : adopted in ramsar(Iran)
  - Examples of Sites in India: Oldest (Chilika Lake, Odisha and Keoladeo National Park, Rajasthan designated in 1981) and Latest (Khichan and Menar, both in Rajasthan designated in 2025)
  - Examples of Wetland City Accreditation (WCA): Indore and Udaipur cities
  - Montreux Record: Ramsar sites where changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring, or are likely to occur due to technological developments, pollution or other human interference. Examples: Loktak (Manipur) and Keoladeo National Park (Rajasthan)
  - Wise use (Ramsar's core idea): keep a wetland's ecological character while people use it (ecosystem approach + sustainable development) → parties do it via national plans + laws + management + public education
  - India at Ramsar COP15 (Victoria Falls, Zimbabwe, 2025): resolution "Promoting Sustainable Lifestyles for Wetlands" (linked to Mission LiFE), backed by 172 countries
  - Unwise use → 74% of J&K lakes vanished or shrank since 1967 (CAG) + native fish gone from Wular + fishers and houseboat owners lose income + heavy metals in fish
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Mangrove cover

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: salt-tolerant trees of the intertidal zone (land–sea <span color="green_bg">ecotone</span>) + 0.15% of the geographical area
- <b>Significance</b>: Store 3x carbon than forests (<span color="green_bg">blue carbon</span>) + Reduce flood depth by 15-20% + Home to over 5700 plant species
- <b>Examples</b>: Sundarbans, Cyclone Amphan 2020 (worked: mangroves cut storm-surge damage = <span color="green_bg">bio-shield</span>) + Mumbai (failed: mangroves lost to reclamation → Bombay HC 2018 declared all mangroves protected forest)
- <b>India's response</b>: India’s initiatives sustainable aquaculture in mangroves + mangrove initiative for shoreline plantation (<span color="green_bg">MISHTI</span> (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes): \* Launched in the 2023-24 Budget.) + SAIME (Sustainable Aquaculture In Mangrove Ecosystem): A pilot project in West Bengal (Sundarbans).
- <b>Challenges</b>: half of the worlds mangroves in danger (most TN and lakshwadeep) + over aqua culture ((Shrimp Farming)) + Coastal Development, Invasive Alien Species, Pollution (Oil Spills), Plastic Waste:+ Agricultural Runoff + Timber and Charcoal: Mangrove wood is highly valued for construction + Sea-Level Rise:
- <b>Way forward</b>: keep them as bio-shields in CRZ and coastal plans + community-led planting (scale MISHTI, SAIME) + shrimp farms outside mangroves + <span color="green_bg">blue carbon</span> credits to pay for protection
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Coral bleaching

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Corals live with algae (<span color="green_bg">zooxanthellae</span>) that feed them → heat, light or nutrient stress → coral throws the algae out → turns white (bleaching)
  - Needs: clean water + 23–29°C + grazers (parrotfish)
  - India: Gulf of Kachchh + Gulf of Mannar & Palk Bay + Lakshadweep + Andaman & Nicobar
- <b>Significance</b>: Why it matters: 25% of marine species + natural breakwater + \~\$10 tn value (tourism, fisheries)
- <b>Examples</b>: Lakshadweep, 2024 (failed: 4th global <span color="green_bg">mass bleaching</span> event hit its reefs hard) + Gulf of Mannar, Vaan island (worked: artificial reef modules slowed island erosion and helped corals recover)
- <b>India's response</b>: India protects via WPA Schedule I + EPA ban on coral and sand use in construction + ICRI membership
- <b>Challenges</b>: Threats: 4th global mass bleaching (NOAA 2024) + coral mining + aquarium trade + ocean acidification
- <b>Way forward</b>: cut runoff + cryobank (Taronga) + Biorock (Gulf of Kutch) + artificial reefs (Tamil Nadu)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Peatlands

- Simply means layers of decaying matter (plants and animals ) decomposing for centuries because no Oxygen so low rate of decomposition ( 1 sq m of peatland holds 5x more carbon than 1 sq m of forest )
- 12 % in world and 60% in india are in danger
- Initiatives: guidelines for global action on peatlands + UNEP global peatlands initiative formed at UNFCCC COP in marakesh, Morocco
- (same vohi problems kya hongi : overuse , over farming ((Palm oil, Eucalyptus).), human acts etc etc. + balancing interest of diverse groups ) + Drained peat is highly flammable (e.g., the massive fires in Indonesia), For fuel or horticulture (gardening soil).
- Way forward: (just ask yourself the question ki what will have to done to protect an area which is under threat)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Marine protected areas

- A specific area where activity is regulated
- Examples in India: Gulf of Mannar marine park, Lothian island (WB) and Gahirmatha (Odisha)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 UNREGULATED SAND MINING

- Sand is the second most consumed natural resource globally after water. In India, rapid urbanization has turned sand into "White Gold," leading to a demand-supply gap of nearly 300 million tonnes annually.
- To make strong concrete, you need riverbed or marine sand.
- Problems : Indiscriminate mining of riverbeds. Altering River Hydrodynamics, Groundwater Depletion, Biodiversity Loss, sand mafia (y? Because low barrier to entry but high profits, sand minor mineral under Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) hence less regulated,
- Law: sand = minor mineral (MMDR 1957) so states regulate + Deepak Kumar v State of Haryana (2012): clearance needed even for small sand mines + EIA 2016 amendment: cluster EIA + District Survey Reports + Sustainable Sand Mining Guidelines 2016 + Enforcement & Monitoring Guidelines 2020 (replenishment rate sets the limit)
- Way forward: national aggregate association (like GAIN) + drones (Telangana model) + <span color="green_bg">replenishment studies</span> (SC)
- Sol : Promoting <span color="green_bg">M-Sand</span> (Manufactured Sand) (artificially created by crushing hard rocks (like granite) into angular sand-sized particles, ecologically safer), The Circular Economy, Tech-Driven Enforcement:
- Analysis of Punjab's Recent Policy Shifts (2025–2026) The Punjab government has moved from a purely prohibitive stance to a regulatory and participatory model: • Landowner Mining Sites (LMS): By allowing farmers to legally mine up to 3 feet of sand on their land, the state aims to decentralize supply and starve illegal cartels. • Crusher Mining Sites (CRMS): Registering crushers as legal mining units reduces the demand for illegally sourced raw materials. • Technological Integration: The use of drone mapping (with IIT Ropar), GPS-tracked vehicles, and an online "Digital Sand Tracking System" reflects a shift toward evidence-based governance
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Coastal sand mining

- Coastal sand mining (beaches + seabed, for building and heavy minerals) → beach and dune erosion + seawater enters aquifers and farms + turtle nesting beaches lost (Olive Ridley, Odisha) + fish breeding grounds damaged → fishers' catch falls
- Second example: Alappad (Kollam, Kerala; mineral-sand mining, "Save Alappad" protest 2019)
- Rules: CRZ notifications ban or restrict it + sand = minor mineral under MMDR 1957, so states regulate + NGT and SC orders against illegal mining

<p>
COASTAL EROSION 
</p>

- Coastal erosion: waves, currents and tides wear away the shoreline → 33.6% of India's coast eroding (worst: West Bengal 63%, Puducherry 57%, Kerala 45%, Tamil Nadu 41%) + coastline re-measured 7,500 → 11,098 km
- Causes: sea-level rise + stronger cyclones and surges + mangroves lost + sand mining and dredging + ports and seawalls block longshore drift + dams cut river sediment
- Effects: land, homes and beaches lost + <span color="green_bg">seawater intrusion</span> + fishers displaced
- Fix: mangroves and sand nourishment + <span color="green_bg">Shoreline Management Plans</span> + CRZ 2019 No Development Zones + Coastal Management Information System + AI monitoring + World Bank K-SHORE (Kerala)

Seawater intrusion

- Seawater intrusion: seawater pushes into coastal aquifers and rivers when fresh groundwater falls
- Causes: over-pumping coastal wells + sea-level rise and surges + dams reduce river flow + sand mining + shrimp ponds and tidal canals
- Eg: Saurashtra and Kutch (Gujarat) + Minjur aquifer near Chennai + Kerala and Sundarbans deltas
- Effects: salty drinking water + farmland salinised + mangroves and freshwater species change
- Remedies: limit pumping (CGWA) + artificial recharge + tidal regulators and check dams (Gujarat's salinity ingress programme) + freshwater injection barriers + mangroves + monitoring wells

COASTAL REGIONS

- Coasts: about 250 mn people within 50 km of the sea + Cyclone Fani about USD 1.2 bn power damage (Odisha 2019, GAR 2025) + half the world's mangroves at severe risk by 2100
- Tools: CRZ 2019 + ICZMP (Odisha, West Bengal) + INCOIS Coastal Vulnerability Index and multi-hazard maps + CMIS + CDRI (IRIS for island states)
- Way forward: mangroves, reefs, dunes as buffers + cyclone-proof housing + shoreline management plans
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 HIGH SEAS TREATY ( Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ agreement) or High Seas Treaty)

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: India signed the treaty but not ratified yet.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: share whatever useful found by any country on sea bed in high seas + creates marine protected areas in high seas + mandates EIA for high sea projects + Finance/ help for developing countries to participate
- <b>Significance</b>: Fills gap in ocean gov, promote equity, strengthen climate resilience, acknowledge indigenous and local knowledge, supports SDG 14 + (30 x 30) target, reinforces India’s support for UNCLOS + Keyword to include : <span color="green_bg">area-based management tools</span>
- <b>Examples</b>: Salas y Gómez and Nazca ridges, SE Pacific (Chile-led, set to be among the first high-seas MPAs) + West African states push the Eastern Atlantic (Canary–Guinea current zone) for the first wave (Jun 2026); first BBNJ COP due Jan 2027
- <b>India's response</b>: Cabinet approved signing (Jul 2024) → India signed (Sep 2024) → ratification still needs a domestic law + treaty in force Jan 2026 after 60 ratifications + fits India's <span color="green_bg">Deep Ocean Mission</span> and SAGAR/MAHASAGAR outlook
- <b>Challenges</b>: not universal ratif, marine protected areas may conflict with territorial claims, Does not establish its own punitive body, Limited Scope: Regarding technology transfer and capacity-building
- <b>Way forward</b>: pass the domestic law and ratify + build deep-sea research capacity to share in the benefits + push for real technology transfer
</toggle>
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h1">
2\. Climate Change

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 NATURAL CAUSES OF CC

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: climate changes that happen without any human role, mostly over thousands to millions of years
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: 1. Continental Drift (affect because of change pod physical features over time)
- 2\. Variation of the Earth’s orbit
- 3\. <span color="green_bg">Milankovitch</span> cycles (Milankovitch cycles are long-term, predictable variations in Earth's orbit, axial tilt, and wobble that alter the distribution and intensity of sunlight reaching our planet. These astronomical shifts operate over tens of thousands of years and are the primary natural drivers behind Earth's historical climate phases, including the onset and retreat of major ice ages)
- 4\. Plate tectonics
- 5\. Volcanic Activity
- 6\. Ocean Currents:Ocean current is one of the major components of the climate system.It is driven by horizontal winds causing the movement of the water against the sea surface.The temperature differences of the water influence the climate of the region.
- 7\. Solar Variability: Sunspot activity can alter incoming solar radiation + Volcanic Eruptions: E.g., Mount Pinatubo (1991) injected aerosols into the stratosphere, causing a short-term cooling of \~0.5°C (Milankovitch cycles work over \~100,000 years, driving cold and warm periods)
- <b>Significance</b>: explain past ice ages, but not the fast warming since 1950 → IPCC AR6: warming is <span color="green_bg">unequivocally</span> human-caused
- <b>Examples</b>: Mount Pinatubo, 1991 (\~0.5°C cooling for about two years) + <span color="green_bg">Maunder Minimum</span> (1645–1715, few sunspots) during the Little Ice Age
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Anthropogenic Factors

- 1\. Greenhouse Gases (water vapour, Co2, CFC, Methane (formed via decomposition of organic matter), Nitrous oxide)
- 2\. Change in land use patterns (From the satellite imagery, it is seen that the clearing of forest cover for agriculture and irrigated farming in arid and semi-arid lands can increase solar energy absorption and the amount of moisture evaporated into the atmosphere)
- 3\. Atmospheric aerosols: what are aerosols ? They are organic and inorganic matter like dust, volcanic ash, water from transpiration, agricultural dust or vehicular emissions, they are very small in size Atmospheric aerosol can: Scatter and absorb the solar and infrared radiation, change microphysical and chemical properties of the clouds, Solar radiation, when scattered, cools the planet
- <b>Examples</b>: Indo-Gangetic Plain winter haze (stubble + vehicles + industry → <span color="green_bg">aerosols</span> cut sunshine and change local climate) + south-east Amazon (2021 study: deforestation turned it into a net <span color="green_bg">carbon source</span>)
- <b>India's response</b>: 3rd largest emitter but low per-capita → <span color="green_bg">CBDR</span> + NDC 2035 + <span color="green_bg">CCTS</span> carbon market + LiFE (see Legal & Policy, <span color="green_bg">Panchamrit</span>)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Legal & Policy Developments

- <span color="green_bg">MK Ranjitsinh</span> vs. Union of India case (2024): Right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.
- India’s enhanced NDC submitted in August 2022, which includes reducing emissions intensity by 45%, achieving 50% non-fossil energy capacity by 2030, and targeting <span color="green_bg">net-zero</span> by 2070.
  - NDC 2031–35 (third NDC): emissions intensity −47% by 2035 (from 2005) + 60% non-fossil power capacity + extra <span color="green_bg">carbon sink</span> 3.5–4 bn t CO₂e
  - Where India stands: intensity −36% by 2020 + 52.57% non-fossil capacity (Feb 2026) + 2.29 bn t sink added by 2021
  - Gaps: \~\$250 bn a year needed till 2047 (NITI) + 50% of capacity but \<30% of generation is non-fossil + coal still \~71% of electricity generated (43% of capacity, \~55% of primary energy) + battery minerals imported
  - Way forward: CBDR-RC finance (green bonds, blended finance) + hybrid solar–wind–storage + agroforestry for sink
- However, on the implementation front, India has already achieved 50% non-fossil electricity capacity as of June 2025—five years ahead of schedule—and has reduced its GDP emission intensity by 36% between 2005 and 2020.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Urgency of Climate Change

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: WHY change is esseential right now ? Because there is seen an acceleration in warming, 0.18 degree from 1990-2015 and then 0.26 degrees warming rate in 2015 to 2025.
- <b>Examples</b>: 2024 = first calendar year above 1.5°C (WMO) + Wayanad landslides after extreme rain (Jul 2024)
- <b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">net zero</span> by 2070 + NDC 2035 (−47% intensity) + 50% non-fossil capacity reached Jun 2025, 5 years early (see <span color="green_bg">Panchamrit</span>)
- <b>Challenges</b>: remaining <span color="green_bg">carbon budget</span> for 1.5°C nearly used up + coal still \~71% of India's power generation + finance gap
- <b>Way forward</b>: global emissions down 43% by 2030 from 2019 (IPCC) + adaptation finance + faster coal phase-down
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Global Temperature Trends

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Rising Global Temperatures: Earth’s surface temperature has increased by \~1.1°C since 1850 (IPCC AR6). The last 8 years (2015–2023) were the warmest on record (WMO 2023), Doubling of CO₂ is likely to cause 2.5–4°C warming. (IPCC AR6)
- <b>Examples</b>: 2024 = warmest year on record and the first calendar year above <span color="green_bg">1.5°C</span> (WMO) + India's 2024 = warmest year since 1901 (IMD)
- <b>Significance</b>: every extra 0.5°C → more heat extremes, heavy rain and droughts (IPCC <span color="green_bg">SR1.5</span>)
- <b>India's response</b>: Heat Action Plans (first: Ahmedabad 2013) + net zero 2070 (see Panchamrit)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Melting Glaciers & Ice Sheets

- Himalayan glaciers (which store Carbon sink (stores 5.4 billion tonnes of carbon) like Gangotri are retreating at \~20 m/year. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have lost over 4000 gigatonnes of mass since 1992, The Hindu Kush–Himalaya region is warming rapidly—0.2 °C per decade over the last 50 years—with projections that 30–67% of glaciers may vanish by 2100 under mid-to-high warming scenarios + Nepal’s Yala Glacier declared dead (if all glaciers melt sea level rise by 60m (NASA) + + Himalayan states reported a loss of 1,072 sq km of forest cover (2019 -2021) + HR (Himalayan region) records about 100 million tourists every year with 240 million expected by 2025. ( indian initiative : NMSHE)
- Melt rate doubled since 2000; Ganga basin −21%, Brahmaputra −16% (<span color="green_bg">ICIMOD</span>) + more dead glaciers: Ayoloco (Mexico 2021), Okjökull (Iceland 2019)
- Why faster: warming fastest at 4,500–6,000 m + <span color="green_bg">black carbon</span> + less seasonal snow + erratic western disturbances
- Effects: less <span color="green_bg">albedo</span> → more warming + about 0.75 mm/yr sea rise (2000–23, WMO) + GLOFs and debris flows (Chamoli 2021, Sikkim 2023, Dharali 2025)
- India: NMSHE + Himansh station + National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme; World: 2025 Year of Glaciers' Preservation + Decade of Action for Cryosphere Sciences 2025–34
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Oceans & Heat Absorption

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Oceans absorb 90% of excess heat, threatening coral reefs and fisheries.
  - Stat: The oceans absorb approximately 30% of anthropogenic CO2.
  - 2025: oceans took in an extra 23 zettajoules of heat (record since the 1960s) + SST \~0.5°C above 1981–2010
- <b>Examples</b>: 2023–24 <span color="green_bg">marine heatwaves</span> → 4th global coral bleaching (NOAA 2024) + warmer Arabian Sea → stronger cyclones on the west coast (Tauktae 2021, Biparjoy 2023)
- <b>India's response</b>: <span color="green_bg">Deep Ocean Mission</span> (2021) + INCOIS ocean monitoring and cyclone/tsunami warnings + <span color="green_bg">MISHTI</span> mangroves + coral restoration + UNOC3, Nice 2025 (<span color="green_bg">Nice Ocean Action Plan</span>: SDG 14 is the least funded SDG) + UN Ocean Decade 2021–30
- <b>Challenges</b>: <span color="green_bg">ocean acidification</span> + oxygen loss + sea-level rise + acidification planetary boundary breached + stratification → less oxygen and nutrients
- <b>Way forward</b>: cut CO₂ + more marine protected areas + ocean goals in the NDC (Blue NDC Challenge: France + Brazil, before COP30)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Extreme Weather Events

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Increase in Extreme Weather Events: India witnessed record-breaking heatwaves in 2022 and 2024.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: <span color="green_bg">ENSO</span>: El Niño and La Niña (ocean) + Southern Oscillation (air)
- El Niño: trade winds weaken → warm water moves to South America → weak
- Indian monsoon, drought + lower kharif yields (rice, sugarcane, oilseeds) + harsher summers
- La Niña: trade winds strengthen → good monsoon + cold winters in the north + more floods and Bay of Bengal cyclones
- <span color="green_bg">Super El Niño</span>: central/eastern Pacific >2°C above normal for a long time (one forecast for late 2026)
- Note: El Niño–monsoon link is weakening (see item 46)
- <b>Examples</b>: Cyclone Biparjoy (2023) and flooding in Himachal Pradesh (2023) reflect this volatility.
- <b>India's response</b>: IMD impact-based forecasts + <span color="green_bg">Mission Mausam</span> (2024) + NDMA heatwave and cyclone guidelines
- <b>Challenges</b>: local extremes (cloudbursts) still hard to forecast + weaker El Niño–monsoon link makes seasonal forecasts harder
- <b>Way forward</b>: Bharat Forecast System + <span color="green_bg">Early Warnings for All</span> (UN, by 2027) + heat and flood plans in every district
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 CO₂ Records

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: A continuous record of CO₂ concentrations since 1958, measured at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii (it has never been 400 ppm in 1000’s of years).
  - In 2024, fossil CO₂ emissions hit an all-time high of 10.2 GtC (up 0.8% from 2023), driven by rising natural gas (+2.4%), oil, and coal use. While US and EU emissions declined, India’s emissions rose to 0.9 GtC.
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: How does Co2 cause climate change : Longwave and short wave differentiation and CO2 absorbs longwave and releases
- <b>Examples</b>: Mauna Loa 2024 average 424.6 ppm, a record (NOAA) + 2023→2024 rise of 3.58 ppm, the fastest ever (Met Office; wildfires + El Niño)
- <b>India's response</b>: 3rd largest emitter, low per-capita → argues <span color="green_bg">carbon budget</span> fairness at COPs + <span color="green_bg">CCTS</span> carbon market (2023) + CCUS push (Budget 2026–27) + 500 GW non-fossil target
- <b>Challenges</b>: emissions still rising (record in 2024) + gas, oil and coal use all up
- <b>Way forward</b>: peak and cut emissions + <span color="green_bg">CCUS</span> for hard sectors + a working carbon market
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Economic Impacts

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: 1 Deg. Celsius warming reduces global GDP by 12 per cent.
- <b>Examples</b>: Kerala floods 2018 (\~₹31,000 cr needed to rebuild, PDNA) + Pakistan floods 2022 (\~\$30 bn <span color="green_bg">loss and damage</span>)
- <b>India's response</b>: SDRF/<span color="green_bg">NDRF</span> + PMFBY crop insurance + Odisha's <span color="green_bg">climate budget</span> tagging + <span color="green_bg">CDRI</span> for resilient infrastructure
- <b>Challenges</b>: adaptation finance gap + most disaster losses uninsured
- <b>Way forward</b>: climate budget tagging in every state + <span color="green_bg">parametric insurance</span> + resilient infrastructure
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Panchamrit – India’s COP26 Climate Goals

- <span color="green_bg">Panchamrit</span> refers to the five key climate goals announced by India at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) to combat climate change and promote sustainability. They are:
  - Reach 500 GW of non-fossil fuel energy capacity by 2030.
  - Meet 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030.
  - Reduce total projected carbon emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030.
  - Cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% by 2030 (from 2005 levels).
  - Achieve <span color="green_bg">net-zero</span> carbon emissions by 2070. (PIB)
  - NITI net-zero report: India 2.9 t CO₂e per person (world 6.7) + \$22.7 tn needed by 2070, gap \$6.5 tn + \~1.3 Gt CO₂e still left in 2070 (farms, cement, heavy industry)

|  | 2015 NDC (2030) | 2022 update (2030) | NDC 2035 | Progress |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Emissions intensity cut (vs 2005) | 33–35% | 45% | 47% | 36% by 2020 |
| Non-fossil power capacity | 40% | 50% | 60% | 52.57% (Feb 2026) |
| Extra <span color="green_bg">carbon sink</span> | 2.5–3 bn t | 2.5–3 bn t | 3.5–4 bn t | 2.29 bn t by 2021 |
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
⚪ Country-Specific Examples

- Canada (2023): Wildfires burned 18.5 million hectares and released 2 gigatonnes of CO₂, nearly three times the nation’s economic emissions and 23% of global wildfire emissions that year.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Challenges & Solutions

- <b>Challenges</b>: Challenges in CC: GHG emissions (India 3rd largest), 8% gap in current policies and NDC’s pledges, the pace of renewable energy growth don’t meet its implementation (power still 70 % coal).
  - Steel sector accounts for about 12% of India’s CO₂. Also: cement \~6% + aluminium \~2.8% of India's GHG → refuse-derived fuel in cement (−80–85% by 2070) + round-the-clock RE for aluminium; EU <span color="green_bg">CBAM</span> makes it urgent
  - CBAM: EU carbon tax on imports from 1 Jan 2026 (cement, aluminium, fertiliser, steel, hydrogen, electricity) → India: trade barrier + cost \~0.05% of GDP (CSE) + hits MSMEs + heavy paperwork → India calls it "disguised protectionism" (see COP30)
  - Methane is responsible for \~30 % global temperature rise since the Industrial Revolution. (Global Methane Tracker, 2025 by International Energy Agency, IEA)
- <b>India's response</b>: Panchamrit + CCTS (2023) + Green Hydrogen Mission + PAT for industry
- <b>Way forward</b>: Solutions: Municipal green bonds (eg. Ahmedabad), move away from FF, invest in battery storage systems, local actions like pachathuruthu initiative (aims to create man-made mini-forests, or "green islands," across the state.), sponge cities (eg. China to avert CC’s flood effects).
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟢 Climate Change & Sea Level Rise

- Sea level rise occurred at 3.3 mm per year (1993 - 2017) in North Indian Ocean.
- Average ocean temprature increased 1.45 degree (water expands when hot leading to sea level rise).
- 2023 driest year for rivers on record.
- On India: Coastal erosion and chronic flooding threaten major cities like Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata. Over 36 million Indians may face persistent flooding by 2100 across a 7,500 km coastline. Over 570,000 hectares could be submerged with a 1-meter rise, displacing about 7.1 million people, while significant infrastructure losses are expected, especially in Odisha and West Bengal. The Sundarbans face serious threats: up to 80% of mangrove cover could vanish, with islands already disappearing and shoreline retreating up to 200 meters annually. Intensifying cyclones like Amphan in 2020 highlight how sea-level rise magnifies storm surges—Amphan pushed seawater 25 km inland, severely impacting the Sunderbans delta. + distress movement eg. of Kosi river and climate change, how it is cutting nearby lands in Bihar, forcing people to relocate (no institutional support, false promises creates trust deficit, no rehabilitation). Lakshadweep faces land submergence risks: Kavaratti, Minicoy may lose 60% of land under RCP8.5.
- Maldives: With average elevations around 1.5 meters, the nation is at risk of becoming largely uninhabitable by 2100 unless adaptive measures are undertaken.
- Bangladesh: Low-lying delta regions could see 0.74 meters of sea rise by 2100, displacing over 2 million people. (Already started)
- Other IOR countries: Sri Lanka (Colombo, coastal belt) + Myanmar (Irrawaddy delta) + Pakistan (Indus delta: <span color="green_bg">seawater intrusion</span> in Sindh) + Indonesia (Jakarta sinking, capital moving to Nusantara) + Seychelles, Mauritius (beaches, reefs, tourism)
- What it means for India: climate migration from Bangladesh into Assam, West Bengal + shared fisheries hit + India as first responder (HADR) + role via <span color="green_bg">CDRI</span> and MAHASAGAR
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 International Court of Justice

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: ICJ case: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), in a landmark advisory opinion “Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change” led by Pacific Island law students (2019); led by Vanuatu, issued on 23 July 2025, declared that nations have a legal obligation under international law—including treaties and customary norms—to curb greenhouse gas emissions and avoid environmental harm. Failing to meet these duties may be deemed an internationally wrongful act, opening the door for reparations such as compensation, restoration, or guarantees against future harm.
- <b>Examples</b>: Vanuatu-led UNGA request (Mar 2023, by consensus) → ICJ opinion Jul 2025 + <span color="green_bg">ITLOS</span> advisory opinion (May 2024: GHG emissions = marine pollution under UNCLOS)
- <b>India's response</b>: at the ICJ hearings (Dec 2024) India argued <span color="green_bg">CBDR</span> + equity + historical emissions of the North → court should not add new duties beyond UNFCCC/Paris
- <b>Significance</b>: first world-court opinion on climate duties → backs <span color="green_bg">climate litigation</span> and loss-and-damage claims
- <b>Challenges</b>: advisory, so not binding + no enforcement
- <b>Way forward</b>: use it in NDCs and finance talks + national courts can rely on it (SC already sees a right against climate change, M.K. Ranjitsinh 2024)
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Migration & Vulnerable Nations

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Panama became the first country to migrate because of climate related effects.
- <b>Examples</b>: Ghoramara island, Sundarbans (failed: about half the island lost to erosion → people moved to Sagar island) + Tuvalu–Australia <span color="green_bg">Falepili Union</span> (2023, worked: climate visas for Tuvaluans)
- <b>India's response</b>: no law for <span color="green_bg">climate migrants</span> yet + resettlement left to states + HADR to neighbours (Bangladesh, Maldives, Sri Lanka)
- <b>Challenges</b>: Most disproportionately affected are small island developing nations (SIDS); had access to only 1 billion out of 100 billion pledged, lost \$153 Billion.
- <b>Way forward</b>: Solutions: Flood barriers (eg. Oyster beds), <span color="green_bg">storm surge</span> modelling and planning, and build flood resistant cities like in South Korea.
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Antarctic & OZONE

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: Ozone: good in the stratosphere (blocks UV), a pollutant at ground level + ODS (CFCs, HCFCs) release chlorine/bromine that breaks ozone → Antarctic hole (Aug–Nov, polar vortex)
  - Recovery to 1980 levels: 2040 world + 2045 Arctic + 2066 Antarctic
- <b>Pillars / key features</b>: Treaties: Vienna Convention 1985 (first to name the problem) → <span color="green_bg">Montreal Protocol</span> 1987 (universal, ODS cut >98%) → <span color="green_bg">Kigali Amendment</span> 2016 (HFCs: not ozone-depleting but strong GHG, cut 80–85% by late 2040s)
  - Antarctica treaty (area south of 60 degree) (use Antarctica only for exploration)
- <b>Examples</b>: Montreal Protocol (worked: ozone layer on track to recover, UNEP–WMO 2023) + India phased out HCFC-141b in foam making by 1 Jan 2020 (among the first developing countries)
- <b>India's response</b>: India: CFCs, CTC, halons out by 2010 + ODS Rules 2000 + HCFC −67.5% + HFC phase-down 10% (2032) → 20% (2037) → 30% (2042) → 85% (2047) + no new HFC plant clearances beyond 2027 + (India operates Antarctic research stations—Dakshin Gangotri (1st), Maitri, and Bharati—and plans Maitri-II, reaffirming its commitment through the Indian Antarctic Act, 2022.)
- <b>Challenges</b>: HFC demand rising with ACs + rogue CFC-11 emissions found in 2018 (eastern China)
- <b>Way forward</b>: <span color="green_bg">India Cooling Action Plan</span> (2019: cooling demand −20–25% by 2037–38) + climate-friendly refrigerants
</toggle>

<toggle heading="h4">
🟡 Impacts – IPCC Draft Report

- <b>Definition & India's status</b>: what warming is already doing to species, oceans, forests, health, gender, migration, farming and schooling (toggles below)
- <b>Examples</b>: Pakistan floods 2022 (1,700+ deaths, 8 million displaced) + Punjab excess rain Jul 2023 → paddy transplanting delayed (more in toggles)
- <b>India's response</b>: NAPCC (9 missions) + <span color="green_bg">State Action Plans on Climate Change</span> + heat action plans + climate-resilient crop varieties (ICAR) + health mission on climate (NPCCHH)
- <b>Challenges</b>: <span color="green_bg">adaptation gap</span>: finance far below need + many ecosystems near the limits of adaptation
- <b>Way forward</b>: National Adaptation Plan + locally led adaptation + early warnings for all

<toggle>
Species

- Extinction rates a thousand times higher than before the Anthropocene + at 2–3°C up to 54% of land and sea species threatened this century + freshwater fish: local biodiversity down up to 75% by 2°C + turtles: upper-range sea-level rise → 59% loss of green turtles’ Mediterranean nesting area, loggerhead 67%
</toggle>

<toggle>
Oceans

- Coral reefs: 70–90% die at 1.5°C + marine heatwaves at least 34% more frequent and 17% longer since 1925 + Arctic summer sea ice down 25% (\~2 million sq km) since late 1970s
</toggle>

<toggle>
Systems
